articles.text: A 2003 Smithsonian Magazine article informs us that Francis Bellamy, the author of the original Pledge of Allegiance, was a Baptist minister’s son from upstate New York. Educated in public schools, he distinguished himself in oratory at the University of Rochester before following his father to the pulpit, preaching at churches in New York and Boston. But he was restive in the ministry (perhaps because he was a socialist?) and in 1891 he accepted a job from one of his Boston congregants, Daniel S. Ford, principal owner and editor of The Youth’s Companion, a family magazine with half a million subscribers. Assigned to the magazine’s promotions department, the 37-year-old Bellamy set to work arranging a patriotic program for schools around the country to coincide with opening ceremonies for the Columbian Exposition in October 1892, the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’ arrival in the New World. The website U.S. History records that the Pledge of Allegiance was written in August 1892 and was originally published in The Youth’s Companion on September 8, 1892. Bellamy had hoped that the pledge would be used by citizens in any country. In its original form it read: “I pledge allegiance to my Flag and the Republic for which it stands, one nation, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.” In 1923, the words, “the Flag of the United States of America” were added. articles.text: City Council adopted the proposed budget for 2022-23, as prepared by the Piedmont Finance Department. City Finance Director Michael Szczech facilitated a public hearing on the proposed fiscal 2022- 2023 budget at the most recent city council meeting on June 6. The city is budgeting $33,864,402 in General Fund expenditures, representing an increase of 7% from last year’s projected expenditures. Salary expenses increased 2% from last year’s projections, and is budgeted at $14,862,826. Maintenance and operations costs represent a quarter of general funds; operation costs are budgeted at $8,603,388, amounting to 24% of the fiscal year 2022-23 General Fund budget. This includes employee related expenses including travel and training, supplies, equipment and vehicle maintenance, contract services, technology services, and various public works services. 2020-2021 was a record year for construction and remodeling costs, increasing 28% over the prior year, and continues to remain high. Staff is projecting to exceed the annual budget this fiscal year by $200,000, or 17%. No changes or additions were made to the proposed budget since June 6. City Council unanimously voted to adopt the budget as is.
articles.title: City Council adopts proposed budget for 2022-23

articles.text: The Alameda County Fair returns this Summer at the Fairgrounds in Pleasanton. The fair is the 7th largest in California. The County Fair continues through July 10 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds, located at 4501 Pleasanton Avenue. A plethora of events will transpire over the course of the fair, including the All-Alaskan Racing Pigs, musical events, movies on the lawn, carnival rides and a “drone show.” The fair is open from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and carnival hours are Wednesday through Thursday, and Friday through Sunday. Every night, a concert will be held at 8 p.m. A list of performers is below. July 2 - Blanco Brown July 3 - The B.B King Experience July 6 - Great White July 7 - Blue Oyster Cult July 8 - CoFunkShun July 9 - Bonfire July 10 - Banda Machos Entertainment at the fair includes a family fun stage, movies on the lawn, live music at the wine garden, and a fireworks display at 9:30 p.m. on July 1 at the Stella Artois Grandstand. Horse races take place every Friday through Sunday, with post time beginning 1:45 p.m. For more details, and to purchase tickets, visit www.alamedacountyfair.com. You can also volunteer at the summer fair. About 900 volunteers of all ages help out at the fair each year. Some of the organizations that volunteers include local schools and colleges, youth groups, garden club members, Girl Scout troops, and performing arts groups. The Alameda County Fair is a local, self-sustaining, non-profit organization. Visit https://annual. alamedacountyfair.com/volunteer/ to learn how to volunteer.

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a Venturing unit with Piedmont Scouts, is expecting to serve pancakes to hundreds of people the morning of Monday, July 4th. Crew Advisor Ken Li confirmed the PCSC members will be in the kitchen at the Veterans Hall cooking and serving breakfast between 8 a.m. and 10:30 a.m. Crew members Maddy Hill and Klara Zietlow serve as co-Vice Presidents of Fundraising and assisted in last year’s pancake breakfast. This year the crew is expecting it will serve over 400 visitors. “We knew we would have a larger event [this year], and Klara and I understood that we would have to dedicate a lot of time to this,” said Hill. “We interact a lot with our [communications department], because we want to get the word out about the event.” “Running a giant fundraising event is nearly impossible if you don’t have the support of a crew or team,” added Zietlow. “PCSC is a great place to gain that experience.” Village Market has donated produce and groceries to PCSC annually for almost a decade, confirmed Li. Piedmont Grocery recently became involved with the fundraiser, and the fundraisMembers of the Piedmont Community Service Crew take over the kitchen in the Veterans’ Hall during the Pancake Breakfast on the 4th of July. ing crew reached out to Starbucks. The crew goes through an application process for donations which vary among the vendors. The crew began the process in late May. “We are on a tight timeframe, but since we have a relationship with Piedmont Grocery and Village Market we can email our [requests] and expedite the process,” Zietlow confirmed. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday through the summer. The compost is first-come, firstserved, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials that can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1 this year requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses to be composted. More information can be found at the City’s news and notifications page. If questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov, tel. (510) 420-3058.

articles.text: After nine years of leading Piedmont Middle School as principal, Ryan Fletcher will be relocating with his family to Denver, Colorado. He will take the position of principal at a small middle school in a suburb outside of Denver. Fletcher earned the unwavering respect of nine years of students to pass through the middle school, his faculty at PMS, and the entire PUSD district. Eighth grade student Sparrow Lieu, a member of Anne Smith’s Yearbook and News Broadcast class, interviewed Fletcher for the PMS Front Page broadcast. A transcript of the interview follows. It was released on the last day of school, June 2. articles.text: Anne Jumper, an incoming senior at Piedmont High School, was awarded a $2,000 Second Place Award in an international art contest on June 15. The Fort Scott, Kansas based competition, is the 7th annual international ArtEffect Project competition, and is put on by the Lowell Milken Center for Unsung Heroes. Jumper and eight other middle and high school winners were challenged artistically to honor unsung heroes with creativity and skill. A total of $16,750 in cash prizes was given out. Jumper’s piece, titled “The Beauty of Genius – Hedy Lamar,” was on display in the Piedmont AP Art show and was featured in the Piedmont Post in May. Her acrylic on canvas painting honors Austrian inventor and actress Hedy Lamarr, whose communication technology prevented the Nazis from intercepting classified messages during World War II. Her innovations are still utilized in Bluetooth and WiFi technology today. “[Hedy Lamar] is a lot like me in that she has taken a lifetime pursuit of art, along with a STEM career and inventing. To see a woman pursue and have such a multi-faceted life at that time was very inspiring to me,” said Jumper in an awards acceptance speech. “You showed how you could skillfully depict her on that reel in so many different expressions and settings,” said Milken Family Foundation Assistant Director Toni Guglielmo. Lowell Milken Center Executive Director Norm Conard said, “Your work is just marvelous. We were blown away with the design itself and putting all this together.” Piedmont High School artist Anne Jumper holds her winning painting of Austrian inventor and actress Hedy Lamarr. “ArtEffect winners submit works of art that show visionary thinking and creative skills of a superior nature,” explained Conard. “We at the Lowell Milken Center for Unsung Heroes salute excellence and the active imagination of our student champions.” The $6,000 Grand Prize went to Chloe Kim, a 10th grader at The Overlake School in Redmond, Washington. Her art focused on Irena Sendler, a Polish social worker who rescued hundreds of children from the Warsaw Ghetto during the Holocaust. To watch Jumper receive the award and explain her piece visit: Youtube.com/watch?v=HOEkpbKEWps LMC also puts on a 2022 Discovery Award Competition, which awards $14,000 to students entering grades 4-12. The submission deadline for projects is July 1, 2022. View competition guidelines and rules at Lowellmilkencenter.org/competitions/ discovery-award

articles.text: Can you remember catching your young child in a lie? For most of us, this experience strikes fear: am I raising a deceitful person? Is this the first step down a dangerous path of dishonesty? Actually, lying is a normal part of cognitive-linguistic development which typically occurs during the preschool years. Studies show that up to 80% of 4-yearolds lie. This milestone indicates that the child has learned that other people have their own and often differing opinions. It signifies that the child has learned that they can use words in a more abstract way than simply to express their needs and wants, namely that words can get someone to think something that is not actually true. The child now understands that what we say does not always correspond with what we are thinking and sometimes we hide what we are really thinking and feeling. To make matters more complicated, this is often the age at which parents may start to encourage lying in certain situations, such as when they receive a present they already have or do not like. Fortunately, many positive traits are associated with this period of language development as well, such as increased communication related to conflict resolution, increased social competence and relationship building. The concomitant emergence of these skills will help parents when attempting to discuss this complicated topic with their little language learners. So, if we view the early Photo Caption: There are positive ways to talk to your toddler about lying. appearance of lying as an important developmental milestone, rather than a morality issue, how can we best react to it? First, it is important to determine the function of the lie. Common functions include: to get something the child wants, to avoid embarrassment, to gain approval or attention, to remove the spotlight from themselves, to spare someone’s feelings, to avoid a consequence or conflict, or poor impulse control. Keeping the truth hidden or creating a “story” often makes the child feel better. Once we have determined the function of the lie, we can discuss it. Resist the impulse to ask “why did you do that?” It is the first question parents go to, and unfortunately it does nothing to increase awareness or insight and adds the negative element of shame. Instead, stick to “what” and “how” questions to review what happened in a supportive and positive way. For example, you can ask what happened first, second, last. You can ask the child how they worked it out. You can discuss what the options were. You can talk about what the child can do differently next time. You can model what you would or would not have done in the situation. And lastly, postponing this kind of a discussion to a later time can allow for a more effective exchange and successful learning opportunity. articles.text: On a sunny Friday afternoon on May 20, members of Cub Scout Pack 5 Webelos started showing up at Boundary campground in Mt. Diablo State Park. When we started to set things up, there were pretty much no completely flat spots for good tent ground, so we took what we could get. When everyone was done setting up, we all played around and talked while the coals warmed up so we could cook our food. Everybody brought a unique foil packet dinner, and everybody enjoyed their foil packet dinner. Once everybody got their share of food, we all played and talked Felix Kansal and Anu Kansal setting up their tent. Nico Wolff helps haul gear to set up for the overnighter on Mt. Diablo. Madison Jung, Anna Benson, and Nico Wolff checking out the views from the summit of Mt. Diablo. some more until we got to, the amazing, s’more time! The kids definitely raided the marshmallows like hungry cattle, but it was all in good fun. I’d say everybody got their fair share of s’mores. After all the sticky and gooey s’mores, I decided to tell a spooky but funny story. Once the story was finished, the whole den got together and did a couple of spooky but still funny skits. articles.text: With the 2022 school year over, high schools throughout the country say goodbye to former student athletes. With that, Piedmont Class of 2023 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their careers as seniors. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them. MORGAN HUNT Soccer & Softball Morgan Hunt is a key member of both the soccer and softball teams. She will be a four-year starter on both teams, a goalkeeper in soccer and outfielder and first baseman in softball. In the recent softball season, Hunt was a power hitter for coach Gene Denard, with six home runs, 18 RBIs on 17 hits with 17 runs scored, and a .279 batting average. She helped the team posy an 18-7 record and win the Shoreline league title with a perfect 10-0 record. She earned a first-team All-League selection and had two in a 4-0 win over Mt. Eden on April 27. On the soccer pitch, Hunt earned another first-team AllLeague selection after helping the team to a 7-5-6 rec record and 5-4-3 against Foothill Division teams. Staff Photos Morgan Hunt is a four-year starter on the softball and soccer teams, earning first-team AllLeague selections in both sports. EMILY FITZGERALD Soccer & Swimming DARIUSH KASHANI Water Polo Emily Fitzgerald was the leading scorer on the soccer team on the winter and also was a member of the swimming team’s 400 freestyle relay and 200 medley relay teams. She will be a four-year starter on Dan Chubbock’s soccer team as a striker, and also as a central attacking midfielder. She helped Piedmont earn the No. 6 seed in the Division 4 NCS playoffs and scored all four goals in the Highlanders’ 4-0 win over No. 11 College Prep on February 26. In the spring she was part of the swim team’s winning 200-medley relay race against Arroyo, and the 400 freestyle relay race versus Encinal and Mt. Eden in April. Dariush Kashani is a four-year starter on the water polo team and earned first-team All-League honors last fall. He was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2020 and 2021 honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year. Kashani was a major factor in the water polo team’s 19-6 overall season and its first-ever WACC Championship title with a 12-8 win over Berkeley on October 30, a game in which he recorded nine saves and one steal. The Highlanders reached the NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seeded team in November but lost 7-4 to No. 2 Marin Academy in a heated defensive game. To get there, they earned a first-round bye and defeated No. 6 Terra Linda 7-4 in the quarterfinals. Emily Fitzgerald was the leading scorer on the soccer team. She scored all four goals in Piedmont’s 4-0 North Coast Section win against neighboring College Prep. Outside the Detention Center reads phrases reflecting the reality for the Chinese immigrants: “Bravery, Loneliness, Frustration, Anger, Segregation, Confinement, Courage, Sacrifice.” There is a $5 admittance cost to enter. The hospital is free to the public and shows the process used to admit Asian immigrants into the country. Along the shore is “The Wharf,” where immigrants took their first steps into the country. You can picture how it might have looked while gazing out to the Bay. Although it’s a beautiful place to rest, it’s a harsh reminder of what immigrants endured upon arrival in the United States. A half mile past the Immigration Station are the abandoned buildings of Fort McDowell, a former soldiers’ barracks, the plush captain’s quarters, and a decrepit building that was once the mess hall. Nearby is the former officer’s building, which is now a museum. Although it is currently closed, a park ranger allowed me inside to take photos. II, old cannon balls, and a section of jail cells. The area is typically open in the busy season around the 4th of July, so be sure to visit. Continuing for nearly three miles along the western side of the Island, you’ll have a constant view of San Francisco, Alcatraz, and the Golden Gate Bridge until reaching the Camp Reynolds Hospital. If you continue off trail past the hospital, a short walk takes you to Point Stuart, which provides a secluded view of the Golden Gate, Sausalito, and Belvedere Island of Marin County. From Point Stuart, it’s just a mile hike back to the starting point where you can wait for the ferry. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California was one of six recipients of the 2022 National Medal for Museum and Library Service, the nation’s highest honor given to museums and library institutions. The medal was awarded by the Institute of Museum and Library Services on June 7. “We are pleased to recognize the outstanding performance and meritorious community and professional service of our six National Medal recipients,” said Institute Director Crosby Kemper. “We look forward to celebrating them and calling attention to their great work not only in their widespread locales but across the land.” Oakland Museum was nominated for the honor by Congresswoman Barbara Lee, explained Oakland Museum CEO Lori Fogarty. “We are deeply honored to receive this award from the Institute of Museum and Library Services and are grateful to our Congresswoman, Barbara Lee, for the nomination,” said Fogarty. “While The Oakland Museum of California this recognition pays tribute to the work and service by the OMCA staff, Board, volunteers and community partners over more than five decades, it is also a call to action for our continued efforts. Museums are more necessary than ever before as places to build connection, trust, and belonging – to foster understanding of our history so we can imagine a more just and healthy future – and this award reminds us of this opportunity and obligation.” Congresswoman Lee described OMCA as a “Museum of the People,” that celebrates the diversity and character of California. “The Oakland Museum of California plays an important role for all of us in learning about the many stories of our State, particularly those stories that are untold and underrepresented,” said Congresswoman Lee. “It is a museum that reflects and uplifts voices from our communities and from our history while also inspiring our future artists, scientists, and history-makers.”
articles.title: Oakland Museum wins national award for Museum and Library Services

Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series, “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. articles.text: In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert on Sunday, July 10 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts celebrating the music of composer Harry Warren. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman (Piano), Rich Trevor (Bass), and Anthony Pegram (Drums), who collectively make up an oldschool, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a tribute to one of the most successful film composers; Warren has composed music for more than 75 films, starring luminaries like Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combo bands and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and pianist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at https://bpt.me/5316993 or at the door. articles.text: The battleground for artistic philosophy is as old as time. They say youth must be served, but I ask: is change for the sake of change obligatory? Jaume Torrent, the noted concert guitarist and composer, observes the following. I found it most apropos, as you will see. An artist’s philosophy of life is one that consists of an unconditional commitment to music. This commitment derives from a vocation that is above economic enrichment and fame. These two objectives, unfortunately, are not in the forefront of all musicians, but they must permeate the spirit that moves our artistic society. Without them we will experience many of the tragedies that humanity continues to experience. Last Sunday Berkeley Symphony presented its final concert of the season. They played up to their usual high standard. Before the actual concert began, the audience was subjected to the usual spoken inanities that have become all too common at concerts these days. The written program notes were excellent. Common sense tells us that we, the audience, can read the program notes for our own intellectual enlightenment, or we can listen to the music and take it at face value. Any more is gratuitous. The concert began with a new piece by Jimmy Lopez Bellido entitled “Rise.” It is a brilliant piece enhanced by an almost Tchaikovsky-inspired orchestration. Exciting and colorful melodies entered and exited making for a most enjoyable listening experience. As the music progressed, I was surprised by the extreme difficulties. It is a fun piece, but the difficulties are daunting. I began to watch individual players in the orchestra. I couldn’t believe my eyes. After the concert was over I talked with some of them whom I know. These are Composer Jimmy Lopez Bellido’s fiendishly difficult work, “Rise”, was performed by Berkeley Symphony at Zellerbach Hall on Sunday as part of the final concert of the season. extraordinary players, and they told me they have never played a piece so difficult in all of their lives. I remember one time in Gregor Piatigorsky’s master class he said to a composer, “You are a very mean man. Why do you write music that is so immensely difficult?” The concert continued with a lofty interpretation of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony. The Berkeley Symphony is a very well-balanced ensemble. The woodwind playing was outstanding. I was especially impressed by the timpani playing of Kevin Neuhoff. In general the strings play exceptionally well, except for some weakness in the first violins. All these things were to the good. The four vocal soloists were in good voice. As most music lovers know, Beethoven made a great departure from precedent when he included the notable poetry of Schiller’s “Ode to Joy.” For some inexplicable reason, Berkeley Symphony chose to include an entirely new script written by Tracy K. Smith. I think the espoused reason is: “This is Berkeley.” Beethoven grappled with his conscience for many years before he wrote his Ninth Symphony. He chose the poetry of Schiller for good reason.

articles.text: Tom Cruise in a scene from Top Gun: Maverick. Top Gun: Maverick, an update of the original film, is now playing in theaters nationwide. It carries the hope that after more than two years of COVID-19 audiences will return to movie houses and to the larger- than-life big screen. Its opening weekends were encouraging; however, I wonder if the box office response to this sequel has more to do with the nostalgic buzz that still prevails 36 years after the original high octane Top Gun was released. The movie wowed audiences and turned Tom Cruise from a well-received actor (Risky Business) into a movie star. But a few words about sequels: When the first movie is as compellingly good as was Tony Scott’s Top Gun, to create a solid, fresh legacy sequel represents a huge, sometimes impossible challenge. The writers have to find a story that feels new, yet has the same intensity as the original. Of course, there has to be an enemy, one that shall not be named, and a hair-on-fire mission crisis involving the swaggering best of the best naval aviators from Miramar Top Gun school flying F-18s and F-35s barely above the hard deck at Mach whatever. Top Gun: Maverick clearly has a bevy of harrowing flight photography moments that makes this film a big screen must. It rips. But to make a complete movie, one that complements the harrowing action, there has to be a narrative that captures the audience. The new cast of characters must have their feet on the ground and not just on the pedals or hands on the stick. In other words, the writers have to find that Top Gun sweet spot. Of course, Maverick is still a captain, still a rebel (it’s pointed out that after almost four decades he should be an admiral), and still a gifted flyer (now a test pilot for the Navy). But in my view the story is thin, the characters vague and not fully developed. articles.text: A scene from Maya the Bee Movie. Released in 2015, Maya the Bee Movie is ideally suited for preschoolers. This animated film features a young apian moppet named Maya (Coco Jack Gillies) and is based on the 1922 children’s book titled The Adventures of Maya the Bee. Maya, raised by a Miss Cassandra (Justine Clark), is by nature curious and adventurous. Against the stern advice of her teacher, Miss C., Maya leaves the hive most mornings to explore the nearby gardens. Ever friendly, Maya engages with a bevy of interesting residents of the flora and fauna. such as dung beetles, ants, spiders and even hornets (considered to be the enemy of the bees). However, given her spunky, motor-mouth personality, and her refusal not to stay put in the hive and do her homework, so to speak, she is soon expelled from the hive by the nasty Buzzlina von Beena (Jacki Weaver). Buzzlina, we learn, is scheming to do away with the Queen of the hive (Miriam Margoyles), and thereby take over the throne, with the help of her dodgy wingman Crawley (Noah Taylor). Maya gets wind of Buzzlina’s nefarious plan to steal the royal jelly and with the help of her friends Flip the violin-playing grasshopper (Richard Roxburgh), and nerdy bee Willy (Kodi Smith-McPhee) tries to upset the plan. The cohort even recruits Sting (Joel Franco), a young hornet, who is, surprisingly, the son of the boss hornet, Hank (Andy McPhee). And with the unexpected help of the hornets, Maya manages to save the hive from Buzzlina. The tension in the story is between the plucky little Maya and friends and the hive’s higher ups, who insist that bees don’t dream and shouldn’t have any fun. They should just keep their noses to the grindstone, work hard, and do as the are told. Maya is a rebel, but still manages to become the heroine of this adventure, preventing a confrontation with the hornets. Maya the Bee Movie will capture the attention of preschoolers who will enjoy this family animated tale. Maya The Bee Movie. Directed by Alex Stadermann. Animation. The 2018 Robin Hood version is meant to satisfy a hip audience that craves a stylized take, given their schooled sophistication with social media and pop culture while feeling most at home in an urban setting. Visually, Robin Hood is a tour de force, with action scenes depicting Robin’s athleticism and his gravity-defying, lethal accuracy with a long bow. One last comment: the dialogue is peppered with verbiage lifted from the gnarly streets of Santa Monica. Characters, such as Friar Tuck (Tim Minchin), say stuff like, “What else you got?” or “I wanna go big.” “This is not going to end well.” Plus I still recall the first voice over line spoken at the beginning of the film: “Forget what you think you know” (about the mythic Robin Hood). articles.text: As readers of my wine column know, Pierre is always in search of a bargain. It’s from the maternal Scottish side of my family. I like nothing better than finding a great French Cote du Rhone or Spanish Garnacha or a Provencal rose at Grocery Outlet for $5.99, but as we all know the term “bargain” is relative. The way a $35 wine can be a bargain is if it tastes as good or better than wines that cost much more. That’s why I am featuring Domain Clavel’s Copa Santa this week. My first experience with this wine was several years ago when I brought it to a blind tasting of my Piedmont wine group. At the end of the evening when the votes were tabulated, the Copa Santa was voted number one wine. When all the wines were revealed we realized it had prevailed over a Cote Rotie, a Hermitage and several Chateauneufs du Pape that were two to four times more expensive than the Copa Santa. That’s why I call it a great bargain. Domaine Clavel is in the Pic St. Loup AVA in the Languedoc region of France. Because it does not have the cache of French regions like Bordeaux, Burgundy or the Rhone Valley, the Languedoc is home to lots of France’s greatest wine bargains. The first vintage of Cope Santa was 1992 and it has become an iconic Languedoc wine since then. It is made of 70% Syrah grapes and 30% Grenache. I was able to obtain a bottle of Domain Clavel’s 2018 Copa Santa. the current release, the 2018 Copa Santa, to see if it was as good as the earlier vintages. The nose of blackberries, cassis and chocolate jumps out of the glass to begin the enchantment. On the palate it is full bodied, hugely rich and packed with plum and dark fruit flavors with a touch of earth. It is layered and complex with good tannin and structure. The finish is long and lingering. The wine is enjoyable now and has the potential to age for two decades. This wine would make a great partner to a cassoulet or a classic French beef daube. Clavel Copa Santa is imported by Pierreclos Imports in Alameda and can be ordered from their website pierreclosimports.com. Check out their other interesting French wine finds while you are there. They offer free shipping with six bottles.

It was another warm summer day on Wednesday, June 15, when 35 walkers and rwo K-9 best friends showed up for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday outing. The walkers hadn’t been to the south side of Piedmont for a few weeks, and it had been over a year since they visited the Davie Tennis Stadium. It’s a unique facility with some history in a beautiful setting. It has been described as a place where time stands still. Visitors always enjoy the stadium with its historic clubhouse. The walkers went to the stadium via Requa Road. They started off going through the top of Piedmont Park past the Community Hall where youth summer camp participants were having fun. Frequent walker Christine Calliste joined the group with eight year old Charles Katzel, so the group’s average age got immediately reduced. The walkers made their way up to Guilford Road, and found the almost hidden, 153-foot path and steps down to Hazel Lane. At Hazel and Requa the walkers saw a large redwood tree that marks the entrance to the Hazel Lane loop. It was noted that this tree also marked the entrance to the first school in Piedmont. Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane, and opened the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls in 1913. Going down Requa Road they saw that an elaborate gazebo which had been damaged in a storm last winter, has been repaired. The group emerged on Wildwood Avenue, went down Prospect Road, onto Oakmont Avenue and then Oak Road to the entrance of the Davie Tennis Stadium. As they walked through its gates the strong smell of eucalyptus trees that surround the stadium welcomed them. It was noted that Frank C. Havens brought eucalyptus to the area from Australia with the idea that the wood would be a fast growing building material replacement for all the redwoods that were cut down during the late 19th and early 20th Century. Unfortunately, the wood proved generally not suitable for lumber as it is quite heavy and shrinks when dry, causong splitting and cracking. Once inside the stadium, more interesting information was shared. Stone quarries were an important part of Oakland’s growth and development. In Oakland’s earliest days, construction materials like stone blocks or paving stones were often used as sailing-ship ballast around Cape Horn. Since much of Oakland’s period of rapid growth occurred prior to the adoption of asphalt in the 1920s, macadam was used extensively in road building. This led to the creation of quarries throughout the area as the city grew. A quarry was opened in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company, and reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892 ta the current site of Davie Tennis Stadium. Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane, and opened the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls in 1913. Going down Requa Road they saw that an elaborate gazebo which had been damaged in a storm last winter, has been repaired. The group emerged on Wildwood Avenue, went down Prospect Road, onto Oakmont Avenue and then Oak Road to the entrance of the Davie Tennis Stadium. As they walked through its gates the strong smell of eucalyptus trees that surround the stadium welcomed them. It was noted that Frank C. Havens brought eucalyptus to the area from Australia with the idea that the wood would be a fast growing building material replacement for all the redwoods that were cut down during the late 19th and early 20th Century. Unfortunately, the wood proved generally not suitable for lumber as it is quite heavy and shrinks when dry, causong splitting and cracking. Once inside the stadium, more interesting information was shared. Stone quarries were an important part of Oakland’s growth and development. In Oakland’s earliest days, construction materials like stone blocks or paving stones were often used as sailing-ship ballast around Cape Horn. Since much of Oakland’s period of rapid growth occurred prior to the adoption of asphalt in the 1920s, macadam was used extensively in road building. This led to the creation of quarries throughout the area as the city grew. A quarry was opened in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company, and reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892 ta the current site of Davie Tennis Stadium. The land was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by former Oakland mayor John L. Davie and his family. It’s from the maternal Scottish side of my family. I like nothing better than finding a great French Cote du Rhone or Spanish Garnacha or a Provencal rose at Grocery Outlet for $5.99, but as we all know the term “bargain” is relative. The way a $35 wine can be a bargain is if it tastes as good or better than wines that cost much more. That’s why I am featuring Domain Clavel’s Copa Santa this week. My first experience with this wine was several years ago when I brought it to a blind tasting of my Piedmont wine group. At the end of the evening when the votes were tabulated, the Copa Santa was voted number one wine. When all the wines were revealed we realized it had prevailed over a Cote Rotie, a Hermitage and several Chateauneufs du Pape that were two to four times more expensive than the Copa Santa. That’s why I call it a great bargain. Domaine Clavel is in the Pic St. Loup AVA in the Languedoc region of France. Because it does not have the cache of French regions like Bordeaux, Burgundy or the Rhone Valley, the Languedoc is home to lots of France’s greatest wine bargains. The first vintage of Cope Santa was 1992 and it has become an iconic Languedoc wine since then. It is made of 70% Syrah grapes and 30% Grenache. I was able to obtain a bottle of Domain Clavel’s 2018 Copa Santa. the current release, the 2018 Copa Santa, to see if it was as good as the earlier vintages. The nose of blackberries, cassis and chocolate jumps out of the glass to begin the enchantment. On the palate it is full bodied, hugely rich and packed with plum and dark fruit flavors with a touch of earth. It is layered and complex with good tannin and structure. The finish is long and lingering. The wine is enjoyable now and has the potential to age for two decades. This wine would make a great partner to a cassoulet or a classic French beef daube. articles.text: Judith Rowe Tulloch passed away on June 15, 2022. A beloved Nana, mom, sister, aunt, and friend, she was a woman who lived life on her own terms. Growing up in Piedmont, she loved spending many a summer at her family’s cabin on the north shore of Lake Tahoe. She worked for Bechtel Corporation for many years and retired in 2000. While she was a longtime Bay Area resident, her work life took her to New York, Alaska, Boston, San Diego, Moscow, and Virginia, among many locations. She was an avid traveler and enjoyed exploring new places and cultures. She was an avid reader and loved attending theatre performances. Affectionately known as “Nana,” one of her greatest joys was spending time with her grandchildren and watching them grow. She loved the art of home decorating and spent a great deal of time creating a warm and inviting space, taking special pride in decorating her home for holidays throughout the year. Her generous nature and huge heart will be remembered by all who knew her. She is survived by her son, daughter-in-law, grandchildren, brother, sisters-in-law, nieces, and many friends. articles.text: Former Piedmont Scout Council president one of only 32 in the U.S. Former Piedmont Scout Council president Anne-Marie Lamarche was named a recipient of the Silver Antelope Award. The award recognizes adult Scouters whose work affects the movement at the territory level. Piedmont is part of Territory 3, covering all of the California and Hawaii. Only two volunteers are recognized from the territory annually. Lamarche has helped guide the territory from a collection of areas into a more cohesive whole, better serving youth and councils who face unique challenges and opportunities here. She served as Territory President and invested countless hours connecting with and guiding leaders throughout this service area. “This recognition is a tribute to Anne-Marie’s tremendous organizational and relationship skills,” said Rob James, a former Piedmont Council president and current territory volunteer. “She has skillfully navigated Scouting through transformations that will strengthen opportunities for youth development.” Lamarche, Piedmont Council’s first female president, has been involved with Scouting for more than 20 years. “Anne-Marie’s leadership and potential was recognized early and she rose through the ranks to successfully lead the territory.” said Wes Smith, a former Piedmont council president and recipient of the Silver Antelope Award. “We are incredibly fortunate with the caliber of volunteer Scouting leadership here in Piedmont,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Our local youth benefit from the wisdom and expertise of 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 Anne-Marie Lamarche recently was presented with Scouting’s prestigious Silver Antelope Award. Anne-Marie and hundreds of others who join her in stepping up.” Lamarche joins Smith, Bob Coleman, and Dale Radcliff as Piedmont Scouters who have been recognized at the Territory level.

A panel of speakers will discuss the documentary process, and will include Sherry Williams, Rheanna Binkley, Bryce Albright, Joanna Black, and Anna Morel. Schnoebelen became involved with the museum in 1989, when the Naval Station was still housed on the island. “At the time it was the 50th anniversary of the Fair, and there were quite a few people still around who had gone to the fair, including artists and architects. A friend and I created a symposium for the anniversary, and included speakers, a slide show, and presentations,” she said. “The museum took special notice of that and invited me to be on the board.” Schnoebelen noted that almost all signs of the World Fair are gone, but that since the museum’s creation in 1975, the City of San Francisco has made earnest efforts to preserve the island’s history. Pied mont resident and museum board member Rebecca Schnier has a special connection to the island. Her father Jacques Schnier created large sculptures for the 1939 World’s Fair which still stand on the island today, preserved by the museum. “What grabbed me was not only the history of my father’s sculptures being there since the late 30s – the historical connection of these beautiful sculptures that I adore, but the history of the island itself. I’m also interested in historical preservation, and as a fifth generation San Franciscan, I was captivated by Treasure Island and all the remarkable things that happened there, starting with the fact that the island itself was actually constructed in the middle of the Bay for the 1939 World’s Fair,” said Schnier, an architect. Her father’s sculptures are on display in front of Building One at the museum. Schnoebelen explained that Building One, where the museum is located, is one of few buildings that will remain among the slew of new developments on the island. Speaker series events held at the museum like “Treasured Stories” help preserve the oral history of Treasure Island, she said. The museum is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.
